Verbal Inspiration
VUR-bul in-SPIH-ray-shun
noun phrase (doctrine of Scripture)
Latin verbalis (of or relating to words, from verbum, word) + English inspiration, from Latin inspiratio (a breathing into); the doctrine that the Spirit's superintendence of the biblical authors extended to the very words they wrote, not merely to their religious ideas or general intentions, so that the words of the original autographs are the words of God expressed through human instruments; the classical formulation is verbal-plenary inspiration, affirming both that the words are inspired (verbal) and that inspiration extends to the whole (plenary)

See also: Verbal Inspiration

Biblical Definition

Verbal inspiration is the doctrine that God's speaking through the biblical authors extended to the very words they employed. When the LORD said to Jeremiah, “I have put My words in your mouth” (Jer 1:9), the promise is word-specific: not “I have given you impressions and let you express them” but “My words in your mouth.” Similarly, when the LORD commissioned Moses, He pledged: “I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall say” (Exod 4:12). Paul grounds the same claim in New Testament apostolic writing: the words communicated are “taught by the Spirit, combining spiritual thoughts with spiritual words” (1 Cor 2:13). The words themselves are Spirit-taught, not merely the concepts. This is the only doctrine consistent with Christ's own exegetical practice: He built arguments on single Greek words and on the tense of a verb (“I am the God of Abraham” — present tense, therefore Abraham lives; Matt 22:32). Deuteronomy 4:2 reveals God's own word-precision: “You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor take from it.” The injunction is word-specific because the revelation is word-specific. Verbal inspiration does not deny human authorship; it insists that the Spirit used each author's vocabulary and literary style providentially and precisely, so that the words produced are the Spirit's own words through human instruments.

Webster 1828 Definition

VERBAL INSPIRATION: the doctrine that the Spirit's superintendence of the biblical authors extended to the very words they wrote, not merely to their ideas or spiritual intentions; grounded in the specific divine word-promises of Jeremiah 1:9, Exodus 4:12, and 1 Corinthians 2:13; paired with plenary inspiration (extending to the whole) to form the standard Protestant doctrine of verbal-plenary inspiration.

VERBAL INSPIRATION. Noun phrase. The doctrine that divine inspiration extends to the words of Scripture, not merely to its ideas, concepts, or spiritual impressions. The mechanism is the Spirit's superintendence of the human authors' word-choice in the original autographs, so that what they wrote is precisely what God intended them to write.

Verbal inspiration is not dictation: the human authors retained their own vocabulary, literary style, personality, and historical context. Paul writes like Paul; John writes like John; the Chronicler writes like the Chronicler. The Spirit's superintendence was entirely consistent with these human differences. But the result — the words actually produced — are the words the Spirit intended.

The doctrinal pair is verbal-plenary: verbal (the words are inspired) + plenary (inspiration extends to the whole canon). Together they form the full Protestant evangelical doctrine endorsed by the Princeton tradition (Hodge, Warfield) and the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978).

Christ's exegetical practice proves the doctrine from the inside: He argued from the tense of a single Greek verb (Matt 22:32) and from a single word in the Psalms (John 10:34–35, “gods”; “Scripture cannot be broken”). These arguments are unintelligible unless the Spirit superintended the very words, not merely the general ideas the human authors intended.

Key Scripture

Jer 1:9 — "Then the LORD put forth his hand, and touched my mouth. And the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth."

Exod 4:12 — "Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say."

1 Cor 2:13 — "Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual."

Deut 4:2 — "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you."

Modern Corruption

Neo-orthodox “dynamic inspiration” locates the Spirit's work in the human authors' religious experience rather than their words; liberal “conceptual inspiration” allows inspired ideas encoded in uninspired and errant words; both positions dissolve verbal inspiration and with it the authority of Scripture's specific claims.

expand to see more

Neo-orthodox theology popularized the category of “dynamic inspiration” (James Orr, then broadly adopted in evangelical liberalism): the Spirit moved the biblical authors spiritually, but the words in which they expressed their inspired experience were their own fallible human productions. The religious insight is divine; the formulation is human and therefore potentially erroneous. On this account, biblical authority lies in the spiritual encounter the text occasions, not in the text's specific propositional claims. The practical consequence is that the specific language of Scripture can be revised, corrected, or overridden whenever the reader judges that a human element has distorted the underlying spiritual insight. The words of Jeremiah 1:9 — “I have put My words in your mouth” — become a spiritual metaphor for divine impulse rather than a specific divine claim about the verbal product.

Liberal higher-critical theology went further with “conceptual inspiration”: God communicated elevated concepts to the prophets and apostles, who then encoded those concepts in historically conditioned and sometimes erroneous language. The cosmology of Genesis 1, the demonology of the Gospels, the eschatological imagery of Revelation — all are culturally relative containers for a timeless spiritual truth. The container can be discarded; the concept remains authoritative. But 1 Corinthians 2:13 rules this out: Paul explicitly distinguishes the words themselves as “taught by the Spirit,” not the ideas alone. The dichotomy between inspired concept and uninspired word is precisely what the New Testament denies.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin verbum (word) + inspiratio (breathing into); the Greek doctrinal basis is Paul's distinction of Spirit-taught words in 1 Cor 2:13, Christ's word-specific exegesis in Matthew 22 and John 10, and Jeremiah 1:9's specific “My words in your mouth”; systematized as verbal-plenary inspiration by the Princeton theologians and the Chicago Statement (1978).

expand to see more

Latin verbum — word, speech; the doctrinal claim is that the Spirit's superintendence extends to the verbum — the actual words — not merely to the mental or spiritual state of the human author; the word is both the human product and the divine result

Hebrew dabar (דָּבָר) — word, thing, matter; the LORD's word (dăbar YHWH) is consistently presented in the prophetic tradition as arriving with verbal specificity: the prophet receives the word and is commanded to speak precisely what was given (Jer 1:9; Ezek 3:4–11; Amos 3:8)

Greek rhēma (ρημα) and logos (λογοζ) — both terms are used in the New Testament for the specific words of divine communication; when Christ says “Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35), He invokes the verbal specificity of the Psalmic text as the ground of His argument

B.B. Warfield (1851–1921), “The Biblical Idea of Inspiration” (1894) — the classic Princeton exposition distinguishing verbal inspiration (the mode) from dictation (which the doctrine does not require) and from dynamic inspiration (which the doctrine rejects); Warfield showed that the New Testament's own appeal to specific OT words and grammatical forms is the strongest evidence for the verbal claim

Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, Article VIII (1978) — “We affirm that God in His work of inspiration utilized the distinctive personalities and literary styles of the writers whom He had chosen and prepared. We deny that God, in causing these writers to use the very words He chose, overrode their personalities”; the classic statement holding verbal inspiration and genuine human authorship together

Usage

"The most powerful argument for verbal inspiration is Christ's own use of Scripture. In Matthew 22:32 He argues for the resurrection from the present tense of “I am the God of Abraham” — a grammatical detail that has no argumentative force unless the tense is exactly what God intended to say. In John 10:34–35 He quotes a Psalmic word (“gods”) and then adds: “Scripture cannot be broken.” The word cannot be broken because it is the Spirit's own word, exact and authoritative. The preacher who undermines verbal inspiration undermines the method his Lord employed."

"Verbal inspiration does not mean wooden uniformity: the Psalms are poetry, the Gospels are narrative, Paul's letters are epistolary discourse, Revelation is apocalyptic vision. The Spirit breathed out the Psalms' metaphors as truly as Paul's doctrinal propositions. The verbal doctrine preserves the full literary variety of Scripture as equally inspired, rather than privileging propositional discourse over poetic or narrative forms as the “more doctrinal” and therefore more inspired portions."

"Practically, verbal inspiration governs how the preacher handles translation: translations are authoritative insofar as they faithfully render the inspired original words. The KJV's accuracy in the verbal tradition is not a claim that the English words are themselves inspired but that they are a faithful transmission of the inspired original words. The preacher's exegetical responsibility is to work back from the translation to the original-language verbal substrate, because the doctrinal and pastoral weight of a text often hangs on a specific word."
